The
"Boiled"

here, represent the new water profile that results
for a water that was boiled to remove temporary
hardness and alkalinity. Where the "original" water
profile might have been more suited for darker beers,
the "boiled" profile may be more suitable for lighter
colored beers. Boiling and decanting water off the
chalky sediment was one of the first water treatment
methods used by brewers. The "
Boiled

Mashing water Calcium content should typically fall in the range of 40 to 100 ppm. Less than 40 ppm calcium content can be used in lager brewing, but the low calcium content may not produce desirable precipitation of trub and oxalates from wort. High oxalates may lead to beerstone formation. Calcium aids in yeast floculation and beer clarification, but calcium is not needed for yeast health (the malt provides all the calcium needed for yeast health).
Calcium should not typically exceed 100 ppm unless it has to be added to provide a desirable anion like sulfate to the water.
If calcium content will be less than 40 ppm, adding the sparging water addition to the mash may elevate the mash calcium content above 40 ppm. Use the
Add Sparging Water mineral additions to the Mash
tool below.

Magnesium is a yeast nutrient, but may be astringent at concentrations over 40 ppm. Preferred range is 0 to 30 ppm.
Malts typically provide sufficient magnesium to wort to provide for proper yeast health and flocculation.
Add magnesium when its bitter and sour taste is desirable in beer, such as in Bitter or Pale Ales. There is no need to add magnesium for other beer styles, even if the water profiles below indicate to. However, using magnesium salts instead of calcium salts can be desirable when you want more chloride or sulfate without driving the calcium concentration too high.

Sodium accentuates beer flavor and roundness at moderate concentrations. Preferred range is 0 to 150 ppm, but should be less than 100 ppm if sulfate content is high. Keeping sodium below 50 ppm is desirable for most pale beers. Higher sodium concentration can be desirable in darker styles.
Sulfate provides a sharper and dryer edge to highly hopped beers.
The preferred range is 0 to 350 ppm, but the concentration
should not exceed 150 ppm unless the beer is highly hopped.
Chloride accentuates fullness and sweetness. The preferred range is 10 to 100 ppm, but the upper limit should be reduced to avoid harshness if the water has high sulfate concentration.

Bicarbonate is an alkaline buffer that limits pH reduction during mashing. It is generally undesirable in beer, but is needed to balance the acidity of dark malts and crystal malts used in some beers.

At least 40 ppm calcium is recommended for oxalate (beerstone)
reduction to occur in the mash. This cell turns
GREEN
when the
calcium content
IN THE MASH
is greater than 40 ppm.
Lager brewers that want to keep their water mineralization low,
can boost calcium content in the mash and rely on sparging water
addition to dilute the overall calcium content in the kettle.
The calcium content in the mash does affect the mash pH.
More calcium will drive the mash pH lower, although acid
addition is a better way to lower mash pH.
The magnesium content in the mash does affect the mash pH. More magnesium will drive the mash pH lower, although acid addition is a better way to lower mash pH.

There is no need for sodium in the mash. However, Baking Soda is an effective way to add alkalinity to the mash. High sodium content in the mash is OK when using Baking Soda since it will be diluted with the sparging water addition. Although high sodium content in the mash is OK, be sure that the sodium content is acceptably low in the
Finished Water Profile
There is no need for sulfate in the mash. Any sulfate
level should be acceptable in the mash, as long as the
level in the
Finished Water Profile
is at the desired level.
There is no need for chloride in the mash. Any chloride level should be acceptable in the mash, as long as the level in the
Finished Water Profile
is at the desired level.

Bicarbonate does not have an ideal range. It is needed only to the extent required to produce an appropriate mash pH.

At least 40 ppm calcium is recommended for oxalate (beerstone)
reduction although lower concentrations can produce good beer
(ie. Pilsen). Lager brewing can benefit from very low calcium
content, however beer taste is often enhanced if the calcium

Sulfate does not have an ideal range, but should generally be below 150 ppm unless the beer is highly hopped. A maximum concentration of 350 ppm is recommended to avoid 'sulfury' aromas in the finished beer although much higher concentrations may be preferred by some tasters.

Sodium Metabisulfite (SMB)

is used as an oxygen scavenger to reduce dissolved oxygen in the wort. It oxidizes to sodium and sulfate ions.
It requires about 6 ppm SMB to eliminate 1 ppm dissolved oxygen. At room temperature, fresh water can contain about 8 or 9 ppm oxygen. At mash temperature, that content drops to about 4 ppm. Preboiling the water and avoiding any subsequent splashing or mixing can reduce the oxygen content to near zero.
Preboiling or deaerating is highly recommended!

Typical SMB dosing for MASHING WATER ranges from 10 to 60 ppm. This calculation assumes SPARGING WATER is always dosed with SMB at 5 ppm over the mashing dose.
Enter 10 ppm SMB dose for systems that have extraordinary oxygen reduction measures including mash caps, deoxygenated water, and no splashing or mixing.
More typical brewing systems might use the upper end of the SMB dosing range.
Be aware that SMB tends to make the perception of roast flavors in beer harsher. Reduction of roast quantities may be necessary to achieve your intended flavor balance.
Enter a SMB dose based on the Oxygen Pickup rate of your system and procedures.

10 ppm is appropriate when oxygen contact is low.
60 ppm is appropriate when oxygen contact is high.
Vary your dose based on those limits.
